**Verse 1:** ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of God." God knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars.﴾

[Page 234]

Since the revelation of this surah followed the dispute between the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy about the Muhajirun, it is clear that the purpose of this verse is an allusion (ta'rid) to the lying and hypocrisy of 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The speech was therefore phrased in a general form that includes all the hypocrites, in order to avoid explicitly naming the intended person. This follows the manner of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?" He meant the owner of Barirah, when he wanted to sell her to 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, and stipulated that the walā' (right of patronage) would belong to him. The verse begins with denying the claim of those whose faith in the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ is being denied, even though that was not the main intent. This signals that God had informed the Messenger of God ﷺ of their inner secrets. It also prepares for what follows, His saying ﴿and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, because the Messenger of God ﷺ knows that the hypocrites said: "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God."

It is possible that their saying ﴿We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God﴾ is reported in meaning (mahkiyyan bil-ma'na), because they say many expressions that convey the meaning that they bear witness that he is the Messenger of God, such as their pronouncing the word of testimony.

It is also possible that they had made a habit of this phrase whenever one of them declared Islam. This is more fitting for reporting their speech with the word "they said" (qalu), rather than with something like "they claimed" (za'amu).

The conditional particle idha (when) is a time adverb referring to the past, as indicated by the fact that both of its clauses are in the past tense. The adverb is connected to the verb "they said" (qalu), which is the response (jawab) of idha.

So the meaning is: You know that they say, "We bear witness that you are the Messenger of God."

The word ﴿nashhadu﴾ (we bear witness) is an emphatic statement (khabar mu'akkad), because testimony (shahadah) is the report of a matter that is certain, since it derives from mushahadah, i.e., direct observation (mu'ayanah). Direct observation is the strongest way of knowing. For this reason, the use of ashhadu and similar verbs of certainty in the sense of an oath has become common, and it has commonly been answered with the same response that an oath receives. This was stated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. The meaning of this is that His saying ﴿nashhadu﴾ is not a performative utterance (insha'). Some exegetes made it a formula of oath, and this is narrated from Abu Hanifah.

[Page 235]

The purpose of His saying ﴿and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ is to inform the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims about a group left unnamed whose trait is hypocrisy, so that they may recognize them, examine their conditions, and test them. The Prophet ﷺ may also receive, through revelation, their identification or the identification of some of them.

Al-munafiqun (the hypocrites) is the plural of munafiq, the one who displays faith and conceals disbelief. This has already been discussed in detail in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The sentence ﴿Indeed you are the Messenger of God﴾ is an explanatory elaboration (bayan) of the sentence ﴿We bear witness﴾.

The sentence ﴿and God knows that you are His Messenger﴾ is an interjected sentence (i'tirad) placed between the two conjoined sentences. This interjection serves to remove the false impression that the listener might get from the sentence ﴿and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, namely that it is a denial of the sentence ﴿you are indeed the Messenger of God﴾. The Muslims at that time were surrounded by groups of hypocrites scattered among them, whose constant concern was to cause strife among the Muslims. Thus the situation required removing this misunderstanding, and this is a kind of precaution (ihtiras).

The verb ﴿yaʿlamu﴾ (knows) is suspended from acting on its object because of the presence of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed) at the beginning of the clause. The grammarians have counted the ﴿inna﴾ in its predicate, the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), among the elements that suspend verbs of the heart from governing. This is based on the view that the lam of the beginning is, in reality, the lam of the response to an oath, and that its proper position is before ﴿inna﴾. However, it was shifted within the sentence out of dislike for the juxtaposition of two adjacent emphatic particles. This was taken from the speech of Sibawayh.

The sentence ﴿and God bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the sentence ﴿they said, "We bear witness"﴾.

Placing the subject (musnad ilayh) before the verbal predicate serves to strengthen the judgment.

The verb ﴿yashhadu﴾ (bears witness) was used in reporting God's denial of them, for the sake of correspondence (mushakalah), so that the nullification of their claim would be equal to their claim.

Falsehood (kadhib) is the contradiction of what a statement conveys with external reality, i.e., actual existence. Therefore the meaning of the hypocrites being liars here is that they are lying in their report about themselves that they bear witness that Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of God, because their statement contradicts what is in their hearts. They do not bear witness to it, and their words do not agree with what is in their souls. By this, the argument of al-Nazzam based on the apparent meaning of this verse is refuted. His view was that falsehood is the contradiction of a statement with the speaker's belief, because he overlooked His saying, "They said, 'We bear witness.'" Al-Qazwini also pointed to this refutation in Talkhis al-Miftah and in al-Idah.

The sentence ﴿indeed the hypocrites are liars﴾ explains (mubayyinah) the sentence ﴿bears witness﴾, like the sentence before it.

Page 236

﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield, and so they have barred (others) from the way of Allah. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing.﴾

This is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because God's refutation of them in their statement to the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], raises in the minds of the hearers the question of their oaths before the Prophet ﷺ that they are believers in him and that they do not conceal hatred for him. So God informed about them that they had taken their oaths as a taqiyya (dissimulation) by which they guard themselves. God has described them as swearing false oaths in many verses of the Qur'an.

Al-junna (shield): that which is used for concealment and protection, and from it the coat of mail is called junna.

The meaning: they made their oaths like a shield by which they guard against whatever harm might reach them. Since the oaths were likened to a shield by way of an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh), this was followed by likening the swearing (of oaths) to the taking of a shield, i.e., using it, so in "ittakhadhu" there is a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). This is not specific to the oath of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy that "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it" [al-Munafiqun: 8], as was mentioned in relating the occasion of its revelation; rather it is more general. For this reason, the correct reading of the plural pronouns in His saying ﴿they have taken their oaths﴾ and so on is in their literal sense, i.e., all the hypocrites took their oaths as a shield; that was their taqiyya, that is, it was a well-known habit among them.

﴿And so they have barred (others) from the way of Allah﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of their barring from the way of Allah upon the false oath, because a sinful oath is among the major sins, for it involves contempt for the rights of God the Exalted; and because when they swore falsely, they thought they had become safe from the Muslims' accusation of them with hypocrisy, so they persisted in disbelief and in scheming against the Muslims, and that is barring from the way of Allah, i.e., turning away from the deeds which Allah commanded to be followed.

The verb (ṣaddū) here is intransitive, whose regular present form would be (yaṣiddu) with a kasra on the ṣad.

The clause ﴿Indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to make their condition appear abhorrent to the hearer. Sa'a is among the verbs of blame, attached to bi'sa, on the premise of transforming the form of its verb from fa'ala (with an open 'ayn) to fa'ula (with a damma on it), for the purpose of conveying blame together with conveying wonder (ta'ajjub) because of that transformation, as Sahib al-Kashshaf pointed out and Sahib al-Tashil alluded to.

[p. 237]

﴿That is because they believed, then disbelieved, so a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not comprehend.﴾

This clause serves as the cause (ʿilla) for the content of the clause ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 2].

The reference to the content of His words ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 2] means: the reason for their proceeding to these evil deeds, at which one is amazed by their wickedness, is their treating the oaths lightly and their returning to disbelief again and again. Thus disbelief became firmly rooted in their souls, their souls grew bold in crimes and pressed on with them, until their hearts became like something sealed upon, so that goodness could not reach them.

So His words ﴿because they believed﴾ are the predicate of the demonstrative ﴿That﴾. The bāʾ (in bi-annahum) has the meaning of causality (sababiyya). Thumma (then) indicates a graded (rutbi) lateness, since abandoning disbelief while displaying faith is greater than open disbelief, and their disbelief is more firmly rooted in them than the display of their faith.

It is also permissible that this lateness is intended in time as well, namely a respite (muhla).

Ascribing the act of believing (āmanū) to them, together with the earlier statement that they are liars in their words ﴿We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], is used in both its literal (ḥaqīqa) and figurative (majāz) senses, since the ranks of the hypocrites vary in hypocrisy and in the severity of disbelief. Among them are those who believed when they heard the verses of the Qur'an, or when lights from the Prophet ﷺ shone upon them, but these did not settle in their hearts.

Then they returned to disbelief, either out of blame from their companions or because of the doubt they cast into their own souls. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This was indeed present." I (Ibn ʿAshur) say: "Perhaps those among this group who repented and whose Islam was sound." For these, the ascription of faith to them is literal.

Among them are those whom the thought of faith passed through, so they wavered and nearly believed, then they turned back on their heels, so the initial state of these resembled the state of the believers when faith occurred to their hearts.

Among them are those who displayed faith falsely, and this is the majority group. What they displayed is not any part of faith at all. God the Exalted has said concerning their like: ﴿and they disbelieved after their Islam﴾ [al-Tawba: 74], so He called it Islam and did not call it faith. And among them are those concerning whom God the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted.'"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. Applying the name of faith to this group is figurative, by the relation of form (ʿilaqat al-ṣūra), and it is like the ascription of the verb yaḥdharu (is wary) in His words, the Exalted: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them﴾ [al-Tawba: 64], in the surah of (Bara'a).

On this consideration, it is permissible that thumma be used in both its original and figurative senses, according to what fits the interpretation of the verb (āmanū).

If the hypocrites are understood as one specific person, namely ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, it is permissible that Ibn Ubayy believed and then disbelieved, so the ascription of (āmanū) is literal, and thumma indicates lateness in time.

The consequence ﴿so they do not comprehend﴾ is attached to His words ﴿they believed, then disbelieved﴾. Thus their disbelief after faith, in the aforementioned respects, became a cause of the evil of their deeds by the requirement of the bāʾ of causality, and a cause of the absence of their perception of theoretical truths by the requirement of the fāʾ of consequence.

Fiqh (comprehension) is understanding of hidden realities.

The meaning is: they do not perceive the indications of faith until they know its truth.

[p. 239]

This is a shift to clarifying some of their conditions which they do not display when they come to the Prophet ﷺ, but which show themselves through observing them. The first clarification began with ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], and this clarification begins with ﴿When you see them﴾ [al-Insan: 19].

The clause ﴿When you see them﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿they do not understand﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3], and it stands in the position of a precaution (ihtiras) and a completion (tatmim), to remove the false impression that someone whose judgment is deceived by their outward appearance might have.

The absence of understanding in their minds is followed by a warning against being deceived by the beauty of their forms, for they are bodies empty of the perfection of souls. This is like the saying of Hassan, and perhaps he took it from this verse:

"There is no harm in the people, in their height and their bulk; their bodies are those of mules, and their minds are those of sparrows."

It also conveys, together with the precaution, an indication of their inner states, such that if the conjunction particle were removed from the two clauses, it would be correct for them to stand in the position of an initial resumptive clause (istinaf ibtida'i). But the conjunction was preferred, to draw attention to the fact that these two are qualities that are reckoned as perfections, while they are defects, because they do not harmonize with what should be a perfection. The beauty of the soul, like the beauty of physical form, is only realized through harmony among its virtues; otherwise a good quality may turn into a cause of deficiency.

The address in this verse is to an unspecified person and includes everyone who sees them and who may think that their forms could deceive him. The Prophet ﷺ is not included in it, because God has informed him of their conditions and made him aware of their identities. It is therefore like the address in His words in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with terror of them﴾ [al-Kahf: 18].

The apparent meaning is that the plural pronoun refers to a specific individual or a limited number, since it is unlikely that all the hypocrites were of beautiful appearance. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "Ibn Ubayy was large-bodied, healthy, handsome, and eloquent of tongue." Al-Kalbi said: "The intended ones are Ibn Ubayy, al-Jadd ibn Qays, and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, who had bodies, appearance, and eloquence." In al-Kashshaf it is said: "And a group of the hypocrites had the same description as Ibn Ubayy, the chiefs of Madinah."

"Ajsam" is the plural of "jism" (body), with a kasra on the jim and a sukun on the sin; it is that which is pointed to, or that which has length, breadth, and depth. It was mentioned in the words of God, ﴿And He increased him in knowledge and physique﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) between the clause ﴿And when you see them﴾ etc., and the clause ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾.

By "listening" in His words ﴿you listen to their speech﴾ is meant giving attention to them, because of the excellence of their articulation and the eloquence of their speech, together with their deceiving, through the sweetness of their meanings, the disguise of their condition upon the Muslims.

Thus the lam in His words ﴿to their speech﴾ is for the implication (tadmin) of the meaning of "tasma'" (you listen) as "tusgh" (you give ear), O listener, since there is no benefit in reporting that one hears speech unless it implies giving ear in order to comprehend their speech.

The clause ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanation (istinaf bayani), in answer to a question that arises from the description of the beauty of their bodies and the fluency of their speech. Since it is in the form of praise, it does not fit with what precedes it, which is their dispraise, so the listener awaits what follows this description.

It is permissible for this clause to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronouns of the third person in His words ﴿when you see them, their bodies impress you﴾.
Its meaning is that the beauty of their forms is of no benefit to themselves nor to the Muslims.

"Khushub" with a damma on the kha and a damma on the shin is the plural of "khashaba" with a fatha on the kha and a fatha on the shin, and it is a rare plural that has been attested only in the word "thamarah"; it is said that "thumur" is the plural of "thimar," which is itself the plural of "thamarah," so "thumur" would be a plural of a plural. Then "khushub" would be in the pattern of a plural of a plural, even though no singular has been heard. It is also said "khushb" with a damma and then a sukun, which is definitely the plural of "khashabah," like "budn," the plural of "badanah."

The majority read it with two dammas. Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub read it with one damma and then a sukun.

"Musannadah" is that which has been propped against a wall or the like, that is, inclined against it. It is thick, long, and strong, but it is not useful for a roof, nor is a wall tied to it. They were likened to propped-up pieces of wood by a comparison of illustration (tashbih al-tamthil), in the beauty of their appearance and the lack of benefit. By this it is conveyed that their bodies, which impress, and their speech, which is listened to, are both empty of benefit, like the emptiness of propped-up pieces of wood of benefit. So when you see them, you reckon them to be people of intellect, courage, knowledge, and understanding. But when you test them, you find them to be other than that, so do not be concerned with them.

* * *

﴿They think every cry is against them﴾.
This clause is in the position of a partial substitute (badal al-ba'd) for the content of the clause ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, that is, from the contradiction between their corrupted inner state and their deceptive outer appearance; that is, they are people of cowardice in the form of brave men.

This is among what this surah has exposed of their hidden thoughts and inner depths, as was mentioned in the preceding verses, although their positions differ due to the variety of the methods of the arrangement of discourse. They share in alerting to their secrets.

"Sayhah" is the single instance of crying out. That is, because of the evil of what they conceal of enmity towards the Muslims, they are constantly apprehensive, fearing that their affair will be revealed to the Muslims. So they are in fear and panic when they hear a cry in a quarrel, or when a lost animal is announced, fearing that this is a raid by the Muslims upon them to strike them.

"Kull" (every) here is used in the sense of "most," because they are only apprehensive out of fear of cries whose causes they do not know, as al-Nabigha used it in his saying:

"In it is every dhayyal (one who drags his robe) and khansa' (a doe), who turns towards every rajjaf (one who trembles) of sand, in the sand dunes."

His words ﴿against them﴾ is a stable adverbial phrase, which is the second object of the verb ﴿they think﴾, and it is not connected to ﴿cry﴾.

* * *

﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾.
This may be a clarificatory resumptive clause (istinaf bayani) arising from the clause ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, because that clause, due to the strangeness of its meaning, raises a question about the cause of their panic and their fear of everything from which the might of the Muslims might be imagined. It is answered that this is because they are fierce enemies of the Muslims who look at the Muslims through the mirror of their own souls. Just as they lie in wait for the Muslims for misfortunes and wish to strike them while showing them affection, so they likewise suppose that the Muslims lie in wait for them and conceal a plan to seize them, in the manner of what Abu al-Tayyib said:

"When a man's deeds are bad, his suspicions become bad, and what he habitually imagines is confirmed."

It is also permissible for this clause to stand in the position of a cause (illah) for the clause ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, on this meaning as well.

It is also permissible for it to be an initial resumptive clause (istinaf ibtida'i) to mention a condition of theirs which it is important for the Muslims to know, so that the branching of ﴿so beware of them﴾ follows from it. In every case, the structure of the speech suffices for the purpose of exposing their inner depths.

The definite article in "al-'aduw" (the enemy) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins) indicating the complete reality of enmity in them, because the most hostile of enemies is the enemy who displays friendship, and he is a flatterer, and beneath his ribs is a deadly disease. On this meaning, the command to beware of them is arranged.

"Al-'aduw" is a noun that applies to the singular and the plural. What is meant is caution against being deceived by their deceiving outward appearances, lest the Muslims come to know their secrets, or accept their advice out of fear of plots.

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ so that he may convey it to the Muslims, and they may beware of them.

* * *

﴿May God destroy them; how are they turned away?﴾
This is a concluding clause (tadhyil), for it has gathered in summary what suffices in place of enumerating their blameworthy qualities, like His words ﴿Those are the ones whom God knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63]. It is driven for the sake of astonishment at the state of their extreme immersion in misguidance and ignorance, through their turning away from the truth.

Thus the astonishment at them begins with a clause whose original form is a supplication for destruction and annihilation, but its use has come to predominate in expressing amazement, or in expressing wonder at the evil condition which its bearer has brought upon himself. For many of the expressions that are supplications for evil are used to express wonder at a hateful act or saying, like their saying: "May his mother be bereaved of him" ("thakilathu ummuhu"), "woe to his mother" ("wayl ummihi"), and "may his right hand be dust" ("taribat yaminuhu"). The use of this in the sense of amazement is a sent metonymy (majaz mursal), because of the mutual connection between the condition reaching evil, the supplication against its owner for destruction, and the amazement at the evil condition. It is thus a connection at two levels, a symbolic metonymy (kinaya ramziyya).

"Anna" here is an interrogative noun about place. The original usage of "anna" is an adverb of place, and it has frequently been made to carry the meaning of interrogation in its uses. It may also be used for figurative place, and it is then explained with the meaning of "how," as in His words ﴿You said: from where is this?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 165] in Surah Al 'Imran, and in His words ﴿From where for them is the reminder?﴾ [al-Dukhan: 13] in Surah al-Dukhan. From this is His saying here ﴿how are they turned away?﴾. The interrogation here is used for astonishment by way of sent metonymy, because a wondrous matter is such that one asks about the circumstances of its occurrence. Thus the asking about it is one of the necessary consequences of its wondrousness. So the clause ﴿how are they turned away?﴾ is an explanation of the general astonishment conveyed by the clause ﴿May God destroy them﴾.

"Yu'faknun" means they are turned away, deflected. It is said: "afakahu," when he turned him away and removed him far. The intended meaning is: He turned them away from guidance, that is, how was it possible for them to turn themselves away from guidance, or how was it possible for those who misled them to turn them away from guidance despite the clear evidence of it.

A parallel of the verse was mentioned in Surah Bara'ah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 63, verse 5:

﴿When it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant.﴾

This is their state of obstinacy, of hostility toward the Messenger (ﷺ), and of turning away from reflecting on the Hereafter, let alone preparing to attain success therein.

"﴿Ta'alaw﴾" is a request from the addressee to come to the one making the request. Its origin is an imperative verb from ta'ali (تَعالى), meaning to force oneself to rise, i.e., to ascend. That sense was forgotten and it came to mean merely a request to come, so it became fixed in one form and turned into an imperative particle (ism fi'l). It was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾ [al-An'am: 151], in the commentary on Surah al-An'am.

This request makes "﴿ta'alaw﴾" indicate that this is one of their states when they are alone among their own group. Thus it is the third of the purposes in explaining the various kinds of those states, and it begins with "idha" (when), just as the two preceding purposes began with "idha": ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], and ﴿When you see them, their bodies please you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4].

The one who said this to them may be some of the Muslims who admonished and advised them, or it may be one of them who was guided and wished to repent.

It has been said that the one addressed was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, in line with the various views mentioned earlier regarding the mention of the hypocrites in the plural form in His saying, ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1] and what follows it.

The meaning is: go to the Messenger of Allah and ask him to seek forgiveness for you. This indicates by implication that what is intended is: repent from hypocrisy, make your faith sincere, and ask the Messenger of Allah to seek forgiveness for you for what has passed from you. So the one who said this to them was aware of their hypocrisy. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, in Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿When it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 13].

The intended meaning of seeking forgiveness is not pardoning the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy: ﴿The mightier will surely expel the weaker from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. This is because Ibn Ubayy went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disowned having said that, and because it does not fit with His saying, ﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6].

"Layy al-ru'us" (ليّ الرؤوس) means inclining them toward a side other than facing the speaker, as a turning away from his speech; that is, they refused to ask forgiveness, either because they remained steadfast in hypocrisy, or because they did not retract what they had said of foul speech against the Muslims, or so that they would not be compelled to acknowledge what was attributed to them of hypocrisy.

The majority of readers recited "﴿lawwaw﴾" (لَوَّوْا) with the first waw doubled, the intensive form of (لوى), to indicate abundance, so it implies that a large number of them turned their heads, meaning a large group of them twisted their heads. Nafi' and Rawh from Ya'qub recited it with the first waw lightened, relying on attributing the verb to the plural pronoun.

The address in "﴿wa ra'aytahum﴾" is to an unspecified addressee, meaning: and you (whoever sees them at that time) see them.

The clause "﴿wa hum mustakbirun﴾" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "﴿yasuddun﴾", meaning they turn away with the turning away of the arrogant from seeking forgiveness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 63, verse 6:

﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾.

This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tariḍa) placed between the description of their conditions, arising from the context of His saying ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], etc.

Know that the construction: sawā'un 'alayhi akadhā am kadhā ("it is the same for him whether this or that"), and similar expressions that have become proverbial, keep these words together with the pronouns suitable to the one spoken of. Its meaning is the equality of the two matters with respect to the one governed by the preposition 'alā, and for this reason it is followed by a clause that explains the aspect of the equality, such as the clause ﴿God will not forgive them﴾, and the clause ﴿they do not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them, they do not believe﴾ [Ya-Sin: 10] in Surat Ya-Sin. As for what is attributed to Buthayna in her lament for Jamil ibn Ma'mar, in her saying:

"It is the same for us, O Jamil ibn Ma'mar, if you die, the hardship of life and its ease."

I do not consider this to be authentically transmitted.

Sawā' is a noun meaning "equal" (musāwin), which in most cases is treated as an invariable noun, so its predicate does not change: we say "they two are sawā'" and "they are sawā'." The form siwā'ayn is anomalous (shādh).

The 'alā in His saying 'alayhim indicates the firmness and settledness of the attribute, so the meaning is: sawā'un fīhim ("equal regarding them").

The hamza in (﴿astaghfarta lahum﴾) is originally the interrogative hamza, with the meaning: "it is the same to them whether the questioner asks about the occurrence of seeking forgiveness for them or asks about its non-occurrence." It is a figurative interrogative used as a metonymy (kināya) for little concern with both states, by the indication of the word sawā'. For this reason the grammarians call this hamza the hamzat al-taswiya (the hamza of equalization). It was previously mentioned at His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6] in Surat al-Baqarah; that is, it is the same to them whether you ask forgiveness for them or not. So 'alā is for figurative elevation, which is firmness and being affected, and it thus returns to the meaning of 'inda (with/before), as you say "it is the same to me whether I am pleased or angry." And His saying ﴿They said, "It is the same for us whether you admonish or are not among the admonishers"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 136] in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The clause ﴿God will not forgive them﴾ is a parenthetical sentence between the clause ﴿it is the same for them﴾ and the clause ﴿They are the ones who say﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. It is a threat against them and a recompense for their contempt for seeking forgiveness from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

* * *

﴿God will not forgive them. Indeed God does not guide the defiant people﴾.

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustan'afa) of initial resumption (istinaf ibtida'i), concerning a state of their conditions.

The clause ﴿Indeed God does not guide the defiant people﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the negation of God's forgiveness for them: God became angry with them and so deprived them of kindness and care.

[Page 246]

This too is among their sayings in their gatherings and assemblies. They said it to their brethren who used to spend on the poor among the Muslims, feigning Islam. It is as if some of them were saying to others: "Make a show of Islam without spending, like their saying: ﴿Come, the Messenger of God will ask forgiveness for you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5]." This verse was followed by that one. It has come in authentic reports that the one who uttered this statement was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, as was mentioned in the introduction to the tafsir of this surah. The attribution of this saying to the hypocrites in general is because they accepted it from him, since he was the head of the hypocrites, or because this saying spread among the hypocrites, and they began to disseminate it among the Muslims.

The position of the sentence is an initial resumptive sentence (al-isti'naf al-ibtida'i), which indicates their deceit and the wickedness of their inner intentions. It moves from describing their aversion when approaching the Messenger ﷺ to describing another kind of their disbelief, namely plotting against the religion under the guise of sincere advice.

The sentence begins with their explicit pronoun rather than relying on the implicit pronoun in ﴿yaqulun﴾ (they say), as a treatment that opposes their intended aim. They concealed their scheme by displaying the intention of sincere advice, so God exposed their matter by greater explicitness, meaning: "We know well that you say this." The explicit pronoun also carries an implicit rebuke, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You are the ones who brought it upon us, so wretched is the abode﴾ [Sad: 60]. Furthermore, the nominal sentence conveys the establishment of the predicate, and the use of the relative pronoun indicates that they were known by this attribute. The imperfect form in ﴿yaqulun﴾ indicates that this statement was repeated by them with the aim of spreading it.

﴿Those who are with the Messenger of God﴾ refers to those who were under his care, such as the People of the Suffa, and those Bedouins who used to join Medina, whom the Messenger of God ﷺ supported during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. Al-Bukhari narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam who said: "We set out with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey during which the people suffered hardship. 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said: Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse from around him." This is a statement of deceit, because its apparent meaning is the intention of sparing the Messenger of God ﷺ the burden of spending on the Bedouins who gathered around him during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, while its inner meaning is the desire to drive the Bedouins away from receiving the prophetic guidance, and from being strengthened by the Muslims through them, or to scatter the poor emigrants so that some of the strength of the Muslims would weaken by their dispersal. The narrations of the hadith of Zayd are mixed (in their wording).

His saying (﴿the Messenger of God﴾) shows that it was uttered by 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and those with him among the hypocrites in this wording, if they said it openly in the presence of the Muslims, since at that time they were feigning Islam.

"Ḥattā" (until) is used here to express causation, by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), because the meaning of ḥattā is the termination of the action mentioned before it, and the end point of an action is when the agent ceases the action upon reaching it. Thus it is a cause of cessation and a reason for it. The intended meaning is not "so when they disperse, then spend on them."

"Al-infiḍāḍ" means to scatter and to withdraw.

* * *

﴿To God belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand﴾.
This is coordinated with the clause ﴿They are those who say: Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God﴾, as a refutation of the hypocrites' scheme in what they intended by their saying, which they displayed as if they meant it as sincere advice to the Muslims. That is: even if their ploy succeeded upon the Muslims, so that they and some of the Muslims withheld spending on the Bedouins and those who take refuge with the Messenger of God ﷺ among the needy, the Messenger ﷺ would not cut off support from them, and this was his custom, as shown by the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "A man came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him to give him something. The Prophet ﷺ said: I have nothing, but borrow on my behalf, and when something comes to me I will repay it. 'Umar said: O Messenger of God, God has not burdened you with what you cannot bear. The Prophet ﷺ disliked 'Umar's remark. A man of the Ansar said: O Messenger of God, spend, and do not fear poverty from the Lord of the Throne. The Messenger of God ﷺ smiled, and cheerfulness was seen in his face at the words of the Ansari. Then he said: I was commanded with this." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Kitab al-Shama'il.

This is a reply by way of refutation (ṭarīqat al-naqḍ), i.e., rebutting their statement, a method in the terminology of the etiquette of debate.

"Khazā'in" is the plural of "khizāna," with a kasra on the kha'. It is the room in which food is stored. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said: Place me over the treasuries of the land﴾ [Yusuf: 55], which was mentioned in the surah of Yusuf. It is also applied, by extension, to the large chest in which wealth is stored, and to book-houses and their cabinets. From this is the saying in the hadith of exchange in the Muwatta': "until my treasurer (khazini) comes from al-Ghaba."

The "treasuries of the heavens" are the places where the causes of obtaining provisions are established: abundant rains, rays of the sun, and beneficial winds, through which fruits and grains are made plentiful, pastures become fertile, and offspring multiply. As for the "treasuries of the earth," they include what is in it of granaries, storehouses and granary-pits, and the treasures of conditions, and what God opens for His Messenger ﷺ of lands, and what is brought to him from the people of the towns.

The "lām" in ﴿lillāhi﴾ indicates ownership, i.e., the disposal of these things belongs to God, exalted is He. Since spending on the poor among the Muslims helps the religion with which God sent His Messenger ﷺ to prevail, the statement that the treasuries belong to God is a metaphor (kināya) for God's facilitating for His Messenger ﷺ the attainment of what he spends from them, as is indicated by his ﷺ saying when the Ansari said (﴿and do not fear poverty from the Lord of the Throne﴾): "I was commanded with this." This is through what God directed to His Messenger ﷺ of the zakat of the Muslims, the spoils of the expeditions, what God opened to him of lands with their bounties, and what God granted him as fay' without fighting.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in ﴿To God belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth﴾ serves to express restriction by reversal (qaṣr al-qalb), and it is a reversal of the implication of their saying, not of its explicit wording. This is because when the hypocrites said ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God﴾, they thought that if they cut off spending on those with the Messenger of God, the Messenger ﷺ would have nothing to spend on them. So God informed His Messenger directly and informed them indirectly that what is with God of provision is greater and more abundant.

The resumption of His saying ﴿but the hypocrites do not understand﴾ (with "but") removes what might be suspected: that when they said ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God﴾, they said it with insight and certainty that cutting off their spending on those who take refuge with the Messenger of God ﷺ would cause their provision to be restricted, so they would scatter from him, based on the premise that the ability to spend is confined to them, since they are the people of means. They had overlooked the multiplicity of causes of wealth and causes of poverty.

The meaning is: they do not perceive the subtleties of what is perceived and its hidden aspects.

The object of ﴿yafqahūn﴾ (they understand) is omitted, i.e., they do not understand that, which is the content of ﴿To God belong the treasures of the heavens and the earth﴾. Or the verb is treated as intransitive, for emphasis on the negation of understanding things on their part in every state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 63, verse 8:

[Page 249]
﴿They say: "If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it." But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers; but the hypocrites do not know.﴾

This is a second resumption (isti'naf) in the style of enumeration and repetition, and for that reason it is not joined by a conjunction. Its like occurs often in contexts of rebuke. This is a description of the evil of their intentions, for they intended threat and the corruption of the sincere bond between the Ansar and their brothers the Muhajirun, by casting this thought into the souls of the Ansar as a seed of strife and division, and by seizing upon a minor dispute that had arisen between two men from the clients (mawali) of the two groups. This statement related here was uttered by 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul when the ally of the Muhajirun struck the ally of the Ansar, as was mentioned earlier in the account of the occasion of revelation of this surah, and at the words of the Exalted, ﴿They are the ones who say: Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. Thus the attribution of the saying to the pronoun of the hypocrites here is like its attribution there.

The use of the present tense (al-mudari') in relating this utterance serves to bring the strange situation vividly before the mind, like His saying, ﴿He argues with us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74]. "Al-Madinah" is their well-known city, which is Yathrib.

"Al-A'azz" means the one strong in honor (al-qawiyy al-'izzah), who is not subdued or overcome, with variation in the degree of honor, since it is among relative matters. Honor is attained through abundance of numbers, breadth of wealth and equipment. By "al-a'azz" he meant the group of the Ansar, for they are the people of Medina and the people of property, and they are more numerous than the Muhajirun. So he intended that the Muhajirun who had come to it would expel the Ansar from their city.

Allah has refuted their words with His saying, ﴿But to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾. This is a reply in the manner called "al-qawl bil-mujib" (accepting the premise) in the science of disputation, and it is among what is called "al-taslim al-jadali" (dialectical concession) in the science of the etiquette of discussion.

The meaning is: if the more honorable expels the more humble, then the believers are the more honorable group. Their honor lies in the Messenger ﷺ being among them and in Allah's support of His Messenger ﷺ and His friends, because the honor of Allah is the true and absolute honor, while the honor of anything else is deficient. Therefore, the friends of Allah are without doubt those who cannot be subdued when Allah wills to help them and has promised them that. And if there is an expulsion from Medina, then it is you, O people of hypocrisy, who will be expelled from it.

[Page 250]
The fronting of the predicate over the subject in ﴿But to Allah belongs honor﴾ is for the purpose of restriction (qasr), and it is a restriction of correction (qasr qalb): that is, honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers, not to you as you suppose.

The repetition of the preposition (al-lam) in His saying ﴿and to His Messenger﴾, although the conjunction would suffice without it, is for emphasis on the honor of the Messenger ﷺ, and that it is due to the honor of Allah and His promise to him. The repetition of the lam also in His saying ﴿and to the believers﴾ is for emphasis as well, since their honor may be hidden while most of them are in a state of paucity and need.

The discussion regarding the digression (al-istidrak) with His saying ﴿but the hypocrites do not know﴾ is similar to what was said just before concerning His saying ﴿but the hypocrites do not understand﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7].

He turned away from the use of the pronoun in His saying ﴿but the hypocrites do not know﴾, although their name had been mentioned in the parallel verse before it, so that the sentence would stand independently in its meaning and move like a proverb.

The negation of knowledge from them here is a declaration of their ignorance for their poor reflection upon the signs of ascendancy and decline. They did not perceive the advance that is in the condition of the Muslims, and the increase of their power day by day, and the diminishing of their enemies. For this is a matter that is witnessed. How, then, could the hypocrites suppose that their honor is stronger than the honor of the tribes of the Arabs, who fall at the hands of the Muslims every time they fight them, from the day of Badr onward?

[Page 251]

This is a transition from disclosing the conditions of the hypocrites, which was presented as a warning against them and a caution about their characteristics, to addressing the believers directly by forbidding them from what could distract them from remembering what Allah has commanded and prohibited. Then comes the command to spend in the paths of good, in the cause of Allah and for the interests of the Muslims and their community, and to help their individuals, so that they are not swayed by the saying of the hypocrites, ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. It also urges hastening to do so before the arrival of death, whose time of coming is unknown, at a moment when one wishes that his term had been delayed so that he could increase in righteous deeds, but wishing will not benefit him. This is a preparation for His saying after it, ﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10]. The occasion for this transition is the relating of the speech of the hypocrites, and for this reason the mention of their sayings was placed before the mention of children, because it is more important according to the context.

[Page 251 continues]

The addressees were called by the relative form (al-mawsul, the relative pronoun construction, ﴿alladhina amanu﴾, "those who believed"), because of what the relative clause indicates of concern for complying with the prohibition.

The wealth and the children were singled out as the objects of the prohibition against being occupied with them in a way that diverts one from the remembrance of Allah, because wealth is something that people often devote themselves to increasing and thinking about acquiring, such that the times spent occupied with it exceed the times spent occupied with children. Moreover, just as it distracts from the remembrance of Allah by devoting time to earning and increasing it, it also distracts from His remembrance by hoarding it, such that the remembrance of what Allah has called for regarding spending it is forgotten.

As for the mention of children, it is an incorporation (idmaj, the inclusion of one element within another's ruling or mention), because being occupied with children, feeling affection for them, managing their affairs and spending times in enjoying their company, is by nature something that causes one to forget the remembrance of Allah's command and prohibition during many times. Thus, being occupied with these two is more than being occupied with anything else.

The speech was framed as directing a prohibition against being diverted from the remembrance, while the intended meaning is the prohibition of their owners, directed at the wealth and the children. This is a well-known usage, and its indicator here is His saying, ﴿And whoever does that, then those are the losers﴾. Its origin is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli, a figure in which a fact is attributed to something other than its true agent) for the sake of emphasis in prohibiting their owners from being occupied through them from the remembrance of Allah. The cause of distraction is therefore treated as if it were the one who distracts, because of the connection between them. This is common in the Qur'an and elsewhere, as in His saying, ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], and in the speech of people: "I will not let you find me doing such-and-such."

The particle "la" in His saying (﴿and not your children﴾) is a negating particle (la nafiyah) conjoining "awladukum" (your children) to "amwalukum" (your wealth). The element conjoined to is the object of the prohibitive "la" (la nahiyah), because a prohibition implies a negation, since it is a request for the absence of an act. The prohibitive "la" originally was the negating "la", which took on the meaning of prohibition when the intent of prohibition was present, and so it governed the verb in the jussive mood, by analogy with the opposing meaning of the imperative "lam" (lam al-amr). Thus the prohibition against being occupied with children was emphasized by the negating particle, so that being occupied with children would have a share equal to that of wealth.

The phrase "dhikr Allah" (the remembrance of Allah) is used in both its literal and figurative senses. It includes remembrance by the tongue, such as prayer and recitation of the Qur'an, and remembrance by the intellect, such as reflection upon His attributes and recalling the obedience to Him. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Better than remembrance of Allah by the tongue is remembrance of Allah at the time of His command and His prohibition."

In this verse is the indication that being occupied with wealth and children that does not divert one from the remembrance of Allah is not blameworthy, and that it has degrees.

[Page 252]

His saying, ﴿And whoever does that, then those are the losers﴾, is evidence for the view of the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that a prohibition demands abstention from an act.

The demonstrative "dhalika" (that) refers to being diverted from the remembrance of Allah through wealth and children; that is, whoever is diverted from the remembrance of Allah, meaning he abandons the remembrance of Allah that He has made obligatory, such as the prayer at its appointed time, and abandons the remembrance of Allah, meaning observing His commands and prohibitions.

Whenever being diverted from the remembrance of Allah occurs through occupation with something other than wealth and children, it is all the more fitting under the ruling of the prohibition and the threat attached to it.

The separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, the pronoun that separates subject and predicate and restricts the predicate) in His saying, ﴿then those are the losers﴾, restricts the attribute of loss to those who do what they were forbidden from. This is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i, a restriction asserted for rhetorical emphasis rather than strict logical exclusivity), for the sake of emphasizing their being characterized by loss, as if the loss of others is not counted as loss in comparison with their loss.

The pointing to them with "ula'ika" (those) is to draw attention to the fact that they deserved what follows the demonstrative because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative, namely, being diverted from the remembrance of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 63, verse 10:

﴿And spend of what We have provided you before death comes to one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous."﴾

This is a refutation and nullification of the scheme of the hypocrites when they said, ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. It is general, encompassing spending on those who gather around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spending on others. Thus the sentence serves as a concluding summation (tadhyil).

The verb (anfiqu, "spend") is used in the sense of a command that includes both the obligatory and the recommended, for the implication of the form "if" (if'al, the imperative), is unrestricted demand, which is the common element between obligation (wujub) and recommendation (nadb).

In His saying (﴿mimma razaqnakum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]) there is an indication that the spending commanded is thanks to Allah for what the spender has been provided with, for gratitude (shukr) is the servant's directing of what Allah has bestowed upon him toward that for which it was created, and this is known from the Shari'ah itself.

The (min) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning "some of what We have provided you." This is a widening (tawsi'ah) from Allah to His servants. Some of this part has a fixed amount, like the rates of zakat and the zakat al-fitr. Among it is what is fixed by meeting an obligatory need in accordance with the spender's capacity, such as the expenses of Hajj, jihad, garrison duty (ribat), the obligatory maintenance of dependents, and the necessary and needed expenses for the public interests of the Muslims. Among it is what is fixed by the fixing of its cause, like expiations (kaffarat). And among it is what He left to people to determine, of what is not obligatory of spending; this is left to people's desires for the reward, for that is a great door of nearness to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. In a hadith: "Charity extinguishes sins as water extinguishes fire."

Allah has reminded the believers of the good in spending, that they must increase in it while they are able, before the loss, i.e., before the impossibility of spending and performing righteous deeds. That is when a person senses a condition that announces the nearness of death and his strength is overcome, so he asks Allah to delay his death and grant him healing, so he may bring much of the good deeds he neglected, hoping that he will be answered. If there is some delay in his term, perhaps Allah will respond to him; if there is no delay in the term, or Allah has not decreed the answer for him, then it is still a great good.

(Lawla) is a particle of urging (tahdid), and tahdid is an urgent, compelling demand. (Lawla) is also used for presentation (ard), reproach (tawbikh), blame (tandim), and wishing (tamanni) figuratively or by metonymy. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Then why was there not a town that believed﴾ [Yunus: 98] in Surah Yunus.

The verb after it should properly be in the present tense, but it came here in the past tense to confirm its occurrence in the supplication of the supplicant, until it is as if it has already come to pass, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The evidence for this is the ordering of the two verbs ﴿fa-assaddaqa wa akun min al-salihin﴾ after it.

The meaning: the believer asks his Lord with urgent request that He bring about the delay of his death until a term in which he can make up for what he neglected of spending and righteous deed.

Describing the term as "brief" (qarib) is a preparation for obtaining the answer, based on common human custom that an easy matter is more likely to be granted by the one asked; this dominates their feelings when they ask Allah, and their souls are drawn by that to what they know. That is why it is reported in a hadith: "None of you should say, 'O Allah, forgive me if You will,' and let him resolve the request, for there is no one to compel Him." This is a warning against this misconception, for the Qur'an relates what people commonly say.

The verb (fa-assaddaqa) is in the accusative by the implied (an) (an-nasb bi-an al-masdariyyah) required after a demand as a response.

As for His saying (wa akun), the readers differed regarding it.

The majority read it jussive (majzum) with the sukun at its end, considering it a direct answer to the demand, since there is no fa' of causation in it, and considering the waw as conjunctive joining one clause to another clause, not joining a single noun to another single noun. This is intended to include in the speech the meaning of a condition in addition to the meaning of causation, so the jazm replaces the conditional verb. Its estimate is: "If You delay me to a brief term, I will give charity and be among the righteous," combining the causation conveyed by the fa' and the conditional suspension conveyed by the jussive of the verb.

Since the first verb is what governs the two verbs, one of which follows the fa' of causation and the other follows the conjunctive waw, the speech conveys causation and conditionality in both verbs, and this returns to the figure of speech called ihtibak. It is as if it were said: "If only You would delay me to a brief term so I could give charity and be among the righteous," meaning, "If You delay me to a brief term, I will give charity and be among the righteous."

Among the subtleties of this usage is that this questioner, after intensifying his request, follows it with the statement that the matter is possible, saying: "If You delay me to a brief term, I will give charity and be among the righteous." This is among the wonders of Qur'anic usage, for the purpose of brevity and abundance of meanings.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and al-Zajjaj directed the reading of the majority by making (wa akun) conjoined to the place (mahall) of (fa-assaddaqa). Abu 'Amr alone among the ten read (wa akuna) in the accusative, and this reading is a mutawatir narration, though it contradicts the orthography of the mutawatir codices (masahif). It has been said that it agrees with the orthography of the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and the codex of Ibn Mas'ud.

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Ibn Mahis also read it so, among the non-famous readings. It was narrated from Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Jubayr, and Abu Raja'. These are less well-known.

Abu 'Amr excused the disagreement of his reading with the codex by saying that the waw was dropped in writing for brevity, meaning they dropped the form of the full vowel of the damma, which is the waw, relying on the pronunciation of the reciter, just as the alif is frequently dropped for brevity in the codices. The Arab readers said: the waw may fall in some orthography, just as they dropped the alif from Sulayman and similar words, i.e., just as they dropped the second waw from Dawud, and they commonly write it Dawud. Al-Farra' said: "I saw in the codex of 'Abd Allah 'fa-qula' (fa-qula) without a waw." All of this is unnecessary, because the Qur'an is transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur), not by the orthography of the codices, and the codices are only an aid to its memorization.

**Page 256**

﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come.﴾ This is a parenthetical insertion at the end of the speech, so the *waw* is *i'tirad* (parenthetical). It serves to remind the believers of the term (*ajal*) set for every spirit (*ruh*) when it is lodged in its body, at the time when the angel who breathes the spirit into it is commanded to record its term, its deeds, its provision, and whether it will be wretched or happy.

The *ajal* is the specific period determined for its life, which cannot be delayed beyond its limit. So when death arrives, the believer's supplication to Allah to delay his term is among the supplications that will not be answered, because Allah has decreed the terms.

This is a great secret, and no one knows the wisdom behind its determination except Allah, the Exalted.

*Al-nafs* means the spirit (*al-ruh*). It is called *nafs* because it is derived from *al-nafas* (with a *fatha* on the *fa'*), which is the air that comes out of the nose and mouth of every living creature that has lungs. The soul is called *nafs* because the breath is generated from it, just as the synonym of *nafs*, *ruh*, is named because it is derived from *al-rawh* (with a *fatha* on the *ra'*), since life (*al-rawh*) comes through it. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said this.

Its *ajal* is the appointed time for its remaining in the human frame.

It is also permissible for *al-nafs* to mean the self (*al-dhat*), that is, the person himself, which is one of the meanings of *nafs*, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. Its *ajal* is then the specified time, its measure, for the remaining of life.

*Lan* is for emphasizing the negation of delay, and the generality of *nafsan* in the context of negation encompasses the souls of believers and others.

The coming of the *ajal* is the arrival of the appointed time for the connection between the spirit and the body. This is what Allah has known of the body's capacity to remain alive according to its strength and its freedom from fatal afflictions.

This is guidance from Allah to the believers, so that they may be ready for death at all times. They should not delay the deed whose reward they desire to obtain. No one who delays a deed that pleases him to do, and to attain its reward, is safe from death coming to him soon or catching him unawares. So he must be extremely cautious against this negligence at all times and in all circumstances, for he may find it impossible to make up for it when the opportunity suddenly passes, or when his capacity weakens. If his soul did not comply with doing righteous deeds before the loss, then how will he wish for a delay of the inevitable term?

* * *

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾
This is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the sentence ﴿Let not your wealth or your children distract you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 9]. Or it is a concluding sentence (*tadhyil*), and the *waw* is parenthetical.

Constructing the report as a nominal sentence (*jumla ismiyya*) affirms the certainty of Allah's knowledge of what the believers do. Since the believers have no doubt about this, the affirmation and reinforcement refer to the necessary implication of the statement, which is promise and threat. The context here is the context of both, because the spending commanded is either obligatory or recommended. Performing it deserves reward, and abandoning the first of them deserves punishment.

The choice of the attribute ﴿Aware (*khabir*)﴾ rather than *'Alim* (Knowing) is because the root *kh-b-r* implies knowledge of hidden matters, to convey that He, the Exalted, knows both what is apparent of deeds and what is concealed, such as the deeds of the heart, which are resolutions and intentions. The placement of this sentence after mention of what death cuts off from the increase of righteous deeds is an indication that whatever death may cut off of the resolve to act, when its time is legally extended, like the lifetime for Hajj for one who is able and does not anticipate an obstacle, and like the preferred time for the prayers, death's prevention of completing it does not diminish the believer's reward. For when a believer habitually performs a portion of worship or resolves on a righteous deed, and then something arises that prevents him, Allah gives him his reward.

Of this kind is that whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, Allah records it for him as a complete good deed, as in the authentic hadith.

**Page 257**

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿what you do﴾ with the second person (*ta'*). Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with the third person (*ya'*), so the pronoun of absence refers back to *nafsan* in the context of negation, because it is general, and so it has the ruling of the plural in meaning.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surah At-Taghabun

This surah is named "Surat al-Taghabun," and it is not known by any other name. This name is not found in any authentic report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, except what Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned from al-Tha'labi, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no child born except that, written on his palm, are five verses from the opening of Surat al-Taghabun." The apparent end of these verses is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [at-Taghabun: 4], so consider it. Al-Qurtubi related it from Ibn 'Umar and did not attribute it with a chain, so perhaps he took it from Ibn 'Atiyyah's tafsir.

The reason for the naming is that the word *al-taghabun* occurs in it, and it does not occur in any other part of the Qur'an.

It is Medinan according to the majority. According to al-Dahhak, it is Meccan. Al-Tirmidhi related from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that those verses were revealed concerning men from Mecca who had embraced Islam and wished to emigrate, but their wives and children refused to let them go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ... (the hadith). Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the case of 'Awf al-Ash'ari, as will come.

It is numbered the 107th in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Jumu'ah and before Surat as-Saff, based on its being Medinan.

Its number of verses is eighteen.

* * *

**Page 259**

Its purposes: This surah includes a reminder that whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth glorifies Allah, that is, declares Him free of deficiencies, with continuous glorification.

And that sovereignty belongs to Allah alone, so He is worthy of being singled out for praise, because He created all of mankind. Some believed in His oneness, and some disbelieved and did not thank His blessings, since He created them in the best form.

It warns them against denying the message of Muhammad ﷺ,

and warns them over that, so that they may take heed from what befell the nations who denied their messengers and rejected their clear signs out of arrogance, refusing to be guided by a human like themselves.

It informs that Allah is Knowing of the apparent and the hidden in the heavens and the earth, so nothing occurs in the world except as His wisdom requires.

It rebuked them for denying resurrection, showed them that it is not impossible, and threatened them that they will meet the recompense for their deeds when they are resurrected. If they wish for salvation, then let them believe in Allah alone, let them affirm His Messenger ﷺ and the Book that he brought, and let them believe in resurrection. For if they believe, their evil deeds will be expiated from them; otherwise their recompense is the Fire, abiding therein forever.

Then it firmly establishes the believers upon what they encounter of harm from the disbelievers, so let them rely upon Allah in their affairs.

It warns the believers against some of their relatives in whom polytheism has penetrated their souls, lest those relatives discourage them from faith and emigration.

It alludes to them with patience over their wealth which the polytheists confiscated.

It commanded them to spend wealth in the ways of good by which they please their Lord, and with the fear of Allah, listening to Him, and obedience.
